Measured verification

What this result establishes

Seam correspondence, current digital geometry, and agreement with analytic deformation cases. These checks do not establish calibrated cloth behavior, self-contact robustness, or a production-ready sewing specification.

From game code to garment code

The useful lesson from one-prompt games is a shared procedural model plus an autonomous loop: generate, run, measure, inspect, correct. A renderer displays the result; a physics solver predicts motion; a pattern model retains the flat material coordinates.

The verified game examples

  • Opus 5.5 · Pelican bicycle, FPS, racing: original short prompts and source. Geometry, textures and audio are generated in code; Three.js is bundled. The author records later mobile fixes.
  • Opus 5.5 · WebGL2 downhill racer: procedural city, no rendering library. One starting prompt; the reported run took 96 minutes and 192 turns.
  • Fable 5.2 · Saltline mirror: inspectable ~1.4 MB HTML, inlined Three.js and procedural assets. It references external Google Fonts. Author-reported eight-hour autonomous run; this is not one inference call.

How this file works

One parameter model creates all four annular-sector panels, their triangle material coordinates, matching seam maps, the 3D cloth mesh and exports. WebAssembly integrates gravity and solves XPBD distance constraints. The four seam pairs share degrees of freedom, preserving the same sewing correspondence under motion. A BVH queries the actual MakeHuman triangles for collision projection; no capsule mannequin substitutes for the mesh.

WebGL2 draws the body and garment using bundled Three.js. The renderer uses procedural weave shading, soft lighting and shadows. The body is anatomical MakeHuman geometry, not a human invented from primitives and not a reconstruction of a particular person. The pinned waist is an explicit support boundary condition.

Heatmaps and CLO conventions

For each triangle, F = Ds Dm⁻¹ maps 2D material to deformed 3D. Eigenvalues of FᵀF yield principal stretch. 100% means no stretch, matching CLO’s strain convention. Stress is calculated from Green strain with an assumed isotropic plane-stress modulus and Poisson ratio, displayed in kPa. It is an estimated material stress, not avatar pressure and not calibrated CLO output.

CLO’s field guide checks sewing lengths, aligned notches, sewing direction, particle distance, collision thickness and skin offset. This demo uses those observable principles. CLO’s proprietary solver and internal certification logic are not reproduced.

Printing and handoff

SVG and DXF are millimetre geometry with a 100 mm calibration square. Solid lines are sewing lines; dashed outlines are 10 mm seam allowances. A4 printing uses 10 mm margins and physical-size tiles. Print at 100%, with browser headers/footers off. Waist and hem are openings; add a waistband, opening/closure, hem finish and fabric-specific tolerances before cutting a production sample.

Asset and library notices

MakeHuman core mesh: CC0 1.0. Three.js and three-mesh-bvh: MIT, notices embedded in this file. Original workbench and solver source: Pattern Agent. No image or audio assets are downloaded. The entire file can be saved and run offline, including its WASM bytes.
